Dottie.headline: Draw it by hand. Without lifting a pencil.

sections.body: Every good idea starts on the back of a napkin. A few boxes. A few arrows. A circle around the part that matters. Dottie keeps that feeling, and puts it on your Mac.

sections.heading: Sketch first. Tidy later.
sections.body: Draw a flowchart, a system diagram or a whiteboard idea in seconds, in a style that looks like you drew it. When it is headed for a document, switch to a clean, precise look with one click. Same diagram. Better posture.

sections.heading: It takes dictation.
sections.body: Dottie speaks MCP, the language AI assistants use to work with your applications. Ask Claude to draw your deployment pipeline from left to right, then ask it to add a staging step. Then watch the shapes appear, as if someone were standing at the whiteboard for you.
Dottie keeps itself up to date, and runs on macOS 14 Sonoma or later. Visit the Phin Tech Store and take one home today.

Dottie.finePrint: Dottie works with Claude and other assistants that support the Model Context Protocol. Pencils sold separately. Not really.

Fanfare.headline: Take home a terminal. Pinstripes included.

sections.body: All along, we've been telling you a terminal can be beautiful. Now we're going to prove it.

Every Fanfare window is drawn the way Mac OS 8.5 and 9 drew one. A black outline. A pinstriped title bar with a close box, a zoom box and a WindowShade box. A Platinum scroll bar with a proportional thumb. A grow box in the corner, right where you left it.

Choose an appearance. Platinum. Copland's Hi-Tech, Gizmo and Drawing Board. System 7 Classic. One-bit Monochrome. Green-screen Phosphor. BeOS, OS/2 Warp, Windows 3.1 and 95, the Amiga's Workbench and Sun's OPEN LOOK.
Inside, it is all business: a modern Ghostty terminal, in Monaco 9, in the Mac's own 16 colours. It just knows how to make an entrance.
The hard part is closing the window.

Fanfare.finePrint: Fanfare is not affiliated with any of the operating systems it admires. Trumpet not included.

Microfiche.headline: Pepper has a lot going on.

sections.body: Walks. Naps. A standing appointment with the mail carrier. A long-term plan concerning the sausage on the top shelf.

Pepper keeps it all in Microfiche, a modal outliner for notes with tasks mixed right in. Every note is a plain-text .fiche file you can keep forever, read anywhere and never lose to a format nobody remembers.
What if a task belongs in a different note? What if the sausage belongs at the top?

Press m to pick up an item, step it to where it should go and press enter. Send it to another note with a keystroke, and both are saved. Jump between headings. Find any command, note or task with the Launcher. Catch a passing thought from anywhere with a global hotkey. It moves like Vim, so your fingers never leave home row. Neither does Pepper, if he can help it.

Every task in every note lands on one Agenda, beside what's on the calendar today. Walks have due dates. Naps repeat. Type :archive and the ones done a fortnight ago are tagged +archived and leave the Agenda, or move to an archive note with every link still pointing at them.
Bring your own help. Press space t a and Claude Code, or any agent that speaks ACP, slides out beside the note, reads it, and writes in it as edits you can undo. Pepper prefers to supervise.
Visit the Phin Tech Store and see how a well-organized dog lives.

Microfiche.finePrint: Pepper's own notebook ships with Microfiche as a sample. No dogs were reorganized against their will.

TwistedPair.headline: Your team has always had good help. Now it can join the meeting.

sections.body: Every team has the same problem: the people who know things and the tools that do things never seem to be in the same room. Twisted Pair puts them at the same table.

sections.heading: Bots are Members, too.
sections.body: Websocket agents, Elixir Extensions and sandboxed Lua Plugins join as Members, under the same access rule and token Scopes as everyone else. No back door. No special treatment. Just one more colleague who never misses a thread.

sections.heading: Threads with titles.
sections.body: All the ease of a chat room, all the findability of a filing cabinet. Threads can be followed, resolved, forked or promoted to a channel of their own. A channel can even be a forum.

sections.heading: Access by Passes.
sections.body: One rule covers invitations, departments and identity-provider groups. Who can see what is never a mystery.

sections.heading: Open, all the way down.
sections.body: Apache-2.0. A published protocol. A server you host yourself and a native desktop client built for speed. Your conversations stay yours.

TwistedPair.finePrint: Twisted Pair needs a Twisted Pair Server, which you host yourself: find it on the Servers shelf, also free. The desktop client is native Rust on GPUI. Cables not to scale.

rabbit-ears-manager.headline: Tonight, the weather is on Channel 1. And so is everything else.

sections.body: Rabbit Ears is a television station of your very own, for every Apple TV, Mac and iPad in the house. Channel 1 is the local forecast, every eight minutes, just the way you remember it.

sections.heading: You're the station manager.
sections.body: Rabbit Ears Manager sets the whole station up from your Mac. Arrange the channels. Sign in to your IPTV providers. Pick the sports. Connect Plex. Configure the relay, so the screens away from home still get the signal.
Make a change once, and Antenna Tower sends it to every screen. Even if the Mac mini takes the night off, each screen keeps its own copy and keeps on playing.
Antenna adjustment not required.

rabbit-ears-manager.finePrint: Requires a Rabbit Ears station. Live TV comes straight from your IPTV providers to each screen. Wood-grain console sold separately.

jeo-paw-dy-player.headline: The answer is: game night.

sections.body: What is the most fun your living room has had in years?

Jeo-paw-dy is a home trivia game show with a late-90s look, hosted by Pepper. The board is on the television. Your phone is the buzzer. An AI judge rules on every answer, and when it isn't sure, the room takes a vote.
Jeo-paw-dy Player lets you join a game that someone else is hosting, right from your Mac. Buzz in. Type your answer, or say it out loud. Argue with the judge. Lose gracefully to a dog.
There are no clues inside, so nobody gets to peek. Not even Pepper.

jeo-paw-dy-player.tagline: Please phrase your answer in the form of a question.
jeo-paw-dy-player.finePrint: Jeo-paw-dy Player needs a game hosted on your network. Contains no clue data. Popcorn sold separately.

herdr-phin-util.headline: One keystroke. Every project, right where you left it.

sections.body: Herdr already keeps your terminals in line. Phin Util teaches it a few new tricks.

sections.heading: Get there in one keystroke.
sections.body: Open a repository, a branch or a pull request without typing a path. Phin Util finds it, clones it if it has to, and puts you in the right directory.

sections.heading: Rooms, ready when you are.
sections.body: Lay out a room once, with the panes, the commands and the windows just so. Then call it up whole, every time.

sections.heading: No Go required.
sections.body: Install it with Herdr's plugin command, or unzip the package and link it. The binaries for macOS and Linux are already inside, checked and ready.

herdr-phin-util.finePrint: Requires Herdr 0.7.4 or later, git, and an authenticated gh. Built for its author; actions may change between versions.

Slaps.headline: You were going to be late. Now you won't.

sections.body: A little notification in the corner is easy to miss. A whole screen is not.

A minute before your meeting, or however long you choose, Slaps covers every screen you own, in every Space and over full-screen apps, with the meeting's title, a countdown and a Join button for its call.
Press Return to join. Press Escape to dismiss. Snooze for a minute, for five, or until it starts.
Prefer a gentler reminder? Choose a banner across the top or bottom of each screen. It won't take the keyboard from whatever you're typing.
Slaps reads the calendars you already keep in Calendar, and finds the Zoom, Meet, Teams, Webex or FaceTime link for you.
Sharing your screen? Slaps holds the alert until you stop, so the whole meeting doesn't learn about your next one.
Reminders with a due time get an alert too, with a Mark Done button. So does your battery: pick a level, and Slaps tells you to plug in before your Mac does it the hard way.
Scripts, Shortcuts and other apps can put up an alert of their own with a slaps:// link or a line of AppleScript. The build finished? You'll know.
Tired of the chime? Have each alert play a YouTube video instead: one of your favourites, a playlist, a channel, or a surprise from ytroulette.com.
Slaps keeps itself up to date, and runs on macOS 14 Sonoma or later. Visit the Phin Tech Store and take one home today.
The hard part is pretending you didn't see it.

Slaps.finePrint: Slaps works with every calendar in the macOS Calendar app. Coffee spills are the user's responsibility.

PhinTechStore.title: Phin Tech Store
PhinTechStore.headline: The whole shop, on your own shelves.

sections.body: Every app on this page, standing on walnut shelves on your Mac. Pick up a box, read its ad, and clip the order form.
Install puts the app in your Applications folder, after checking it against its published checksum. An older copy goes to the Trash, never to oblivion.
Boxes with a newer version wear an Update sticker. Update All takes care of every one at once.
New apps arrive on the shelves on their own, ads and all, and the store keeps itself up to date while you sleep.
The hard part is choosing.

PhinTechStore.finePrint: The Phin Tech Store runs on macOS 14 Sonoma or later. Walnut shelving not included with every Mac.

Welty.headline: Remember when you checked your mail, and then you were done?

sections.body: Once, mail was a program on your own computer. It came when you asked, it stayed where you put it, and nobody else had a say in how it looked.

Welty brings that back for your Fastmail and Gmail accounts. Your mail is kept in a database on your Mac, so it opens at once and reads just as well on an airplane. File it, flag it or archive it offline, and Welty makes the changes as soon as you're connected again.

sections.heading: Two looks. One mail program.
sections.body: Choose Classic, with windows straight out of a 1999 desktop, or Modern, with today's controls. Both have the same features and the same keys.

sections.heading: Your hands never leave the keyboard.
sections.body: Use Gmail's keys or Vim's: j and k to move, x to check a message, v to check a run of them, g and a letter to change mailboxes. Archived the wrong thing? Take it back before Welty has even sent the change.

sections.heading: Unsubscribe with one keystroke.
sections.body: Welty finds the unsubscribe link in each newsletter, and where the sender allows it, unsubscribes without opening a page.

sections.heading: Help is standing by.
sections.body: An AI agent can read your mail through Welty, file it, and draft your replies. Each draft opens in a window for you to finish. Welty only sends mail when you click Send.
Dark mode, too. Mail that wasn't made for it is darkened, and a company's blue stays blue.

Welty.tagline: Mail, the way you remember it.
Welty.finePrint: Welty works with Fastmail and Gmail accounts and runs on macOS 14 Sonoma or later. Stamps not required.

TwistedPairServer.title: Twisted Pair Server
TwistedPairServer.headline: Every good conversation needs a room. This is the building.

sections.body: Twisted Pair Server is where your team's conversations live: every Channel, every Thread, every Member and every Bot, on a computer you choose, under a roof you own.

sections.heading: A workgroup in a box.
sections.body: The server and its Postgres database come together, and start with a single docker compose command. Choose a password and two secrets, start it, and sign in as the first administrator. Then make a one-time link for each new Member from the Admin row. Each person chooses their own password.

sections.heading: No per-seat licenses.
sections.body: Twisted Pair is Apache-2.0. Bring the whole department, and their robots, too. Bots join as Members, under the same Passes and token Scopes as everyone else.

sections.heading: Plugins included.
sections.body: With the GitHub Plugin, every pull request becomes a titled Thread, with a live card that follows CI and deploys and a Take Review button. The Thread resolves itself on merge.

sections.heading: System requirements.
sections.body: Any Mac or Linux computer that runs Docker. Postgres 17 is included. For Members outside the office, a TLS proxy or a Cloudflare Tunnel.

TwistedPairServer.finePrint: Twisted Pair Server needs Twisted Pair, the desktop client, which is sold separately (also free). Server closet not included.

herdr-phin-picker.title: Phin Picker
herdr-phin-picker.headline: Every project. One keystroke.

sections.body: Press ⌘O in Herdr and every project you have is in front of you, the ones you use most at the top.
Type a few letters to narrow it down. Press Tab for its branches and worktrees. Press Enter and you're there, in a Space of its own.
What if it's a pull request?
Paste the link. Phin Picker clones the repository if you don't have it, makes a worktree on the branch and opens it. A whole stack of pull requests opens as one Space, a tab for each layer.
Paste a GitHub issue or a Linear ticket, and you get a branch named for it. Type org: to browse a whole organization.
It never leaves home row. Neither does your train of thought.

herdr-phin-picker.finePrint: Phin Picker is a mod for the Herdr desktop app. It needs git, and gh signed in for pull requests and issues. Keys are added only where they're free.

redpen.headline: Somebody, somewhere, is waiting on you.

sections.body: Three repositories asked for your review this morning. One of them asked twice. Meanwhile your own pull request has been approved since Tuesday, and nobody thought to mention it.

sections.heading: Everything that needs you, in one list.
sections.body: Red Pen gathers every pull request asked of you, by name or by your team, from GitHub, Forgejo and Gitea. Your own are sorted by whose move it is. Put one off until Monday and it comes back on Monday, not a minute before.

sections.heading: Notes in red ink.
sections.body: Press c to read the changes. Write notes on the lines as you go, keep the ones that are only for you, and press p on the ones worth saying. ⌘Return posts them as one review. Next time, ⇧S shows only what's new since you looked.

sections.heading: An agent who has read the code.
sections.body: Open the Agent panel with your own Claude Code, Pi or ACP agent. It reads the diff, then the rest of the repository: the callers, the definitions, the tests. It reads the log of the check that failed. Ask, and it walks you through the change stop by stop, on the lines themselves.

sections.heading: Before it's a pull request at all.
sections.body: ⌘O opens a branch in a clone on your Mac, perhaps one an agent is still writing. Mark it up the same way. Your notes go back to the agent as a round of review, and never to the Forge.

sections.heading: Never leave the keyboard.
sections.body: j and k to move, a slash to filter, Space for every command in the app. The lists, the changes and the agent all answer to the same keys.
Visit the Phin Tech Store and get your reviews back before anyone has to ask twice.

redpen.finePrint: Requires macOS 14 Sonoma or later. Sits quietly in your menu bar and keeps count. Signs in with your own token, or with gh. The agent is your own Claude Code, Pi or ACP agent, sold separately. Red ink not included.

Cubicle.headline: Your desktops, finally with names.

sections.body: Every Mac has extra desktops. Almost nobody uses them, because nobody can remember which one is which. Cubicle gives each desktop a name, a place on a grid and a keystroke, so you always know where you left your work.

sections.heading: Jump. Don't swipe.
sections.body: Switching desktops on a Mac means a long, lazy slide across the screen. Cubicle skips it. Press a key and you are there. Press another and a grid of all your desktops appears. Type a few letters of a name, "ino" for "Innopts" say, and Cubicle finds it for you.

sections.heading: It plays well with others.
sections.body: Cubicle comes with a command for your terminal, so a script can say "cubicle go code" and be there before it finishes the sentence. There is a workflow for Alfred: type @ and a few letters of a name and off you go. And it installs with Homebrew, because of course it does.
Cubicle lives in your menu bar, keeps itself up to date, and runs on macOS 13 Ventura or later. Visit the Phin Tech Store and take one home today.

Cubicle.tagline: A place for everything. And a name for every place.
Cubicle.finePrint: Cubicle needs the Accessibility permission to press keys on your behalf, and promises to use it only for good. The Alfred workflow needs Alfred's Powerpack. Cubicles sold separately. Corner offices not included.

corkboard.headline: Some work only makes sense on a wall.

sections.body: You know the wall. Index cards, push pins, string from one card to another, and one person who can explain it. Linear keeps your team's work very well. It just never let you pin any of it up.

sections.heading: Press b.
sections.body: Corkboard pins the Issues you're looking at to a cork board, a column for each Workflow state. Every Link between two of them is a String from tack to tack, coloured by what it means, and it swings when you move a card. Drop a card in another column and Linear hears about it.

sections.heading: Hands stay home.
sections.body: j and k to move. l b to say what's blocking it, l p to give it a Parent, p p to put it in a Project. Space shows every Command and ⌘K finds one. The mouse works too, for those who insist.

sections.heading: Or read it as a page.
sections.body: Press P and the same Issues are written out as a Microfiche Note: a Heading for each state, each Sub-issue beneath its Parent. Corkboard opens Microfiche folders as well, with the same keys.

Corkboard keeps a copy of your Issues on your Mac, so lists, filters and Search answer at once, on a plane or off one, and your edits wait in line until Linear can take them. Visit the Phin Tech Store and get it all up on the wall.

corkboard.finePrint: Corkboard needs macOS 14 Sonoma or later and a Linear personal API key, which it keeps in the Keychain. Push pins not included.

boiler-room.title: Boiler Room
boiler-room.headline: Somebody has to keep checking. It doesn't have to be you.

sections.body: The support case says someone will be in touch. So you look. You look again after lunch, at four, at six, and once more before bed, just in case. Nothing. Nothing. Nothing.

Boiler Room does the looking. Write a script that checks once, the way you'd type it in a terminal, and Boiler Room runs it every three hours, or every two minutes, or at nine on weekdays. It keeps what the script said every time.
It only speaks up when something's different. A new reply, a build gone red, a status that finally moved: one notification. The other forty-one times, not a word.
When a script needs you, it asks. Rotate the key? Yes or No, from the notification. It waits.
Waiting on a pull request? Type boiler-room submit --every 30s -- gh pr checks 123 and get on with your day. Boiler Room tells you when it passes, then tidies up after itself.
Visit the Phin Tech Store and take your evenings back.

boiler-room.tagline: Somebody's got to watch the gauges.
boiler-room.finePrint: Boiler Room needs macOS 14 Sonoma or later. The scripts are yours; Boiler Room only runs them. Full-screen alerts need Slaps, also from Phin Tech. Coal not included.
